questions.prompt: What does this program print?
questions.explain: `p = &a` makes `p` point to `a`; `*p = 7` writes through the pointer, so `a` becomes 7.
option_notes: That was a's value before the assignment through the pointer.
`%d` prints the int value, not an address.

questions.prompt: An `int *p` holds the address 0x2000 and `sizeof(int)` is 4. What address does `p + 3` hold?
questions.explain: Pointer arithmetic is scaled by the size of the pointed-to type: `p + 3` is 3 * 4 = 12 bytes further, 0x2000 + 0xC = 0x200C.
option_notes: Adding 18 is neither 3 nor 12; hex 12 is 0x0C.

questions.prompt: Which expressions are equivalent to `v[2]` for an array `v`?
questions.explain: `a[i]` is defined as `*(a + i)`, and addition is commutative, so `*(2 + v)` and even `2[v]` work. `&v[2]` and `v + 2` are the ADDRESS of the element, not the element.
option_notes: Same thing with the operands swapped.
This is a pointer to v[2], not its value.
Also a pointer, not the value.

questions.prompt: Put these three lines in the right order to swap `*a` and `*b`.
questions.explain: Save one value first, overwrite it, then store the saved value in the other place. Any other order loses a value.

questions.prompt: What does this program print?
questions.explain: `p = &b` makes `p` point to `b`; `*p = 9` then writes into `b`. `a` is never touched.

questions.prompt: What does this program print? (A pointer to a pointer.)
questions.explain: `*pp` is `p` and `**pp` is the int `p` points to, which is `x`.

questions.prompt: What does this program print?
questions.explain: `p` points to v[1]. Pointer arithmetic moves by whole elements, and negative indices are legal while they stay inside the array.

questions.prompt: What does this program print? (The difference of two pointers.)
questions.explain: Subtracting two pointers into the same array gives the number of ELEMENTS between them (not bytes): 5 - 1 = 4.

questions.prompt: What does this program print? (On a 64-bit system.)
questions.explain: `sizeof(s)` is the size of the POINTER (8 bytes on 64-bit systems), while `strlen(s)` counts the 5 characters of the text.

questions.prompt: What does this program print? (A pointer to a function.)
questions.explain: `int (*f)(int, int)` declares `f` as a pointer to a function taking two ints and returning an int. Calling `f(2, 3)` calls `add`.

questions.prompt: What happens when a program reads or writes through a `NULL` pointer?
questions.explain: `NULL` points to no object. Dereferencing it is undefined behaviour; on Linux it normally stops the program with a segmentation fault.
options: Undefined behaviour, in practice usually a crash (segmentation fault)
It reads the first byte of the program
option_notes: Nothing is guaranteed to be there.

questions.prompt: Why can you not dereference a `void *` directly (`*p` where `p` is a `void *`)?
questions.explain: `void *` is a generic address without a type. Convert it to a typed pointer first (`*(int *) p`). (A course slide shows `void *a` dereferenced in a swap function: that code does not compile.)
options: The compiler does not know the size or type of what it points to
You can: it gives an int
option_notes: A void pointer has no type to give.

questions.prompt: Which statements make `p` point to the first element of `int v[4]`?
questions.explain: The array name converts to a pointer to its first element, and `&v[0]` is that address. `*v` and `v[0]` are the first element's VALUE, an int, not an address.
option_notes: That is an int, not a pointer.
That is an int, not a pointer.

questions.prompt: The operator `*` applied to a pointer (`*p`) is called the {{0}} operator.
questions.explain: `*p` follows the pointer to the object it points to; `&x` does the opposite (the address of x).

questions.prompt: What is wrong with `char *s = "abc"; s[0] = 'x';`?
questions.explain: A string literal lives in read-only memory. Use an array (`char s[] = "abc";`) when you need to change the text.
options: It modifies a string literal, which is undefined behaviour (usually a crash)
option_notes: It compiles, but it is wrong.

questions.prompt: Which declaration makes `f` a pointer to a function that takes an `int` and returns an `int`?
questions.explain: The parentheses around `*f` matter: `int *f(int)` declares a FUNCTION returning a pointer to int.

questions.prompt: After this code runs, what is `p`?
questions.explain: `x` lives only inside the braces. After them its memory can be reused, but `p` still holds the old address: using it is undefined behaviour.
options: A dangling pointer: it points to a variable that no longer exists
option_notes: It stores an address, not the value.

questions.prompt: Sort each expression by what it produces, for `int a[3]; int *p = a;`.
questions.explain: `*` and `[]` follow a pointer and give the element; `&` and pointer arithmetic produce addresses; the array name converts to the address of its first element.

questions.prompt: Match each declaration with its meaning.
questions.explain: Read declarations from the name outwards. `const` before the `*` protects the pointed-to value; after the `*` it protects the pointer.
pairs: pp points to a pointer to an int
p points to an int that cannot be modified through p
p itself cannot be changed to point elsewhere

questions.prompt: Put the steps of using a pointer to a heap block safely in order.
questions.explain: Always check the result of `malloc` before using it, and release the block exactly once.
items: Declare the pointer and set it to NULL
Check that malloc did not return NULL
Use the memory through the pointer
free the block and set the pointer to NULL

questions.prompt: A `char *a` holds the address 0x10000000. What does it hold after `a++`?
questions.explain: Pointer arithmetic moves by `sizeof(*a)` and `sizeof(char)` is 1 by definition in C. (A course quiz may give 'depends on the size of char' as its answer; in standard C it never does.)
options: It depends on the size of a char on the machine
option_notes: That would be an `int *` with 4-byte ints.
Always 1: sizes are measured in chars.
